title: Étale Fundamental Groups and Cohomology
summary: This library describes algebraic covering spaces through their geometric fibers and studies the sheaves they carry, relating fundamental groups to Galois actions and explaining selected cohomological obstructions.
overview: Over a field, an étale scheme can be recovered from its geometric fiber together with the action of the field's Galois group. For a general scheme, finite étale covers are likewise described by finite locally constant sheaves and, on a connected base with a geometric point, by fundamental-group actions. The results explain when changes to a scheme preserve its covers and how its fundamental group combines geometry with the arithmetic of the base field. For a proper scheme over a separably closed field, extending the field to another separably closed field preserves its finite étale covers and its geometric fundamental group.

The cohomological results describe what can be recovered from local data. The Kummer sequence records the obstruction to extracting a global root, while the selected Hilbert 90 theorem expresses the triviality of line bundles over a characteristic-zero field. Finite direct image is exact, commutes with arbitrary base change, and preserves cohomology in every degree. For a proper scheme over a henselian local ring, restriction to the closed fiber is an isomorphism on H⁰ and injective on H¹ for arbitrary module coefficients. The general higher-degree proper base change and Lefschetz trace formula remain further goals.
scopeNote: The proper constant-field theorem gives an equivalence of finite étale covers over separably closed field extensions. Finite direct image is treated in all cohomological degrees. The general proper henselian comparison here gives H⁰ bijectivity and H¹ injectivity, not H¹ surjectivity, the full higher-degree proper base change theorem, or the general specialization equivalence. A full Lefschetz trace formula is a separate goal.

entries.title: Étale schemes over a field as continuous Galois sets
entries.summary: The geometric fiber over a separable closure gives an equivalence for all étale schemes over a field, including those with infinitely many components.
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $K$ be a separable closure of $k$, and equip $G=\operatorname{Aut}_k(K)$ with its Krull topology. There is an equivalence
$$\operatorname{Et}/k \simeq G\text{-}\mathbf{Set}_{\mathrm{disc,cont}}.$$
On the right are discrete sets with continuous $G$-action; on the left are schemes étale over $\operatorname{Spec}k$.

The forward functor takes the geometric fiber over $\operatorname{Spec}K$. No finiteness condition is imposed on the entire scheme or the entire Galois set. Continuity nevertheless forces every individual orbit to be finite.
discussion: Finite Galois orbits correspond to finite separable extensions, while arbitrary disjoint unions account for schemes with infinitely many components. This makes the étale geometry of a point accessible through field Galois theory and provides the basic model for fundamental groups of schemes. Grothendieck's SGA 1 seminar of 1960–61 developed that passage from field extensions to finite covers of schemes.
history: Grothendieck's SGA 1 seminar of 1960–61 extended field Galois theory to finite covers of schemes. The classification over a field is the starting example; Stacks Project Lemma 58.2.2 includes arbitrary étale schemes.

entries.title: The exact sequence of geometric and arithmetic fundamental groups
entries.summary: For a geometrically connected, quasi-compact, quasi-separated scheme over a field, the geometric fundamental group is the kernel of the natural map to the absolute Galois group.
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $L$ a separable closure, and $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ a quasi-compact, quasi-separated scheme such that $X_L$ is connected. Choose a geometric point $\xi:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to X_L$, with $\Omega$ separably closed, and let $x$ be its image in $X$. Then
$$1\longrightarrow\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(X_L,\xi)\longrightarrow\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(X,x)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)\longrightarrow1$$
is exact.

The maps are the continuous homomorphisms induced by pullback and the structure morphism. Exactness includes injectivity on the left, surjectivity on the right, and equality of the kernel with the image. No splitting is asserted.
discussion: The sequence separates the geometry over separably closed constants from the arithmetic of the base field, while explaining how both enter a single fundamental group. It does not choose a splitting. This geometric–arithmetic viewpoint was developed in SGA 1; purely inseparable invariance relates the separable-closure formulation here to the algebraic-closure formulation in the Stacks Project.
history: The geometric–arithmetic sequence is part of the fundamental-group theory developed in SGA 1. Stacks Project Lemma 58.14.3 gives the algebraic-closure formulation; purely inseparable invariance relates it to the separable-closure formulation.

entries.title: Finite étale covers are invariant under universal homeomorphisms
entries.summary: An integral, universally injective, surjective morphism induces an equivalence of finite étale cover categories and hence the expected pointed fundamental-group isomorphism.
statement:
Let $f:X\to Y$ be integral, universally injective, and surjective. Pullback induces an equivalence
$$f^*:\operatorname{FinEt}(Y)\simeq\operatorname{FinEt}(X).$$
Such a morphism is a universal homeomorphism.

If $X$ and $Y$ are connected and $\xi:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to X$ is a geometric point, with $\Omega$ separably closed, the induced homomorphism is a topological group isomorphism
$$\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(X,\xi)\cong\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(Y,f\xi).$$
Its underlying map is exactly the usual fundamental-group homomorphism associated with $f$.
discussion: Nilpotent structure and purely inseparable changes can alter a scheme without altering its finite covering theory. This permits passage to reduced schemes or purely inseparable models in fundamental-group calculations, even though constructions involving the full structure sheaf may change. Known as topological invariance of finite étale covers, the result is formulated for universal homeomorphisms in the Stacks Project.
history: This property is known as topological invariance of finite étale covers. Stacks Project Proposition 58.8.4 formulates it for universal homeomorphisms, encompassing both nilpotent thickenings and purely inseparable phenomena.

entries.title: Finite étale covers of proper schemes are invariant under separably closed field extensions
entries.summary: Extending a separably closed ground field preserves finite étale covers of a proper scheme and the actual geometric fundamental group.
statement: Let $K/k$ be an extension of separably closed fields and let $X$ be a proper $k$-scheme. For the projection $p:X_K\to X$, actual pullback gives an equivalence
$$p^*:\operatorname{FEt}(X)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{FEt}(X_K).$$

Every finite étale cover of $X_K$ therefore descends to $X$, and morphisms between such covers descend uniquely. For any geometric point $\xi$ of $X_K$, the projection induces a continuous group isomorphism
$$\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_K,\xi)\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,p\xi).$$
No smoothness, reducedness, or connectedness assumption on X is required. The comparison is natural under further extensions of the coefficient field and morphisms of the original proper schemes.
discussion: This permits the ground field to be enlarged for geometric calculations while preserving all finite étale covering data. The construction proves essential surjectivity for the actual pullback functor, so it supplies descent of covers as well as comparison of existing ones.

The Stacks Project records the algebraically closed case as Lemma 58.9.3. The formalization extends it to separably closed fields using invariance under purely inseparable changes, and identifies the resulting fundamental-group isomorphism with the projection-induced map.
history: Invariance of finite étale covers under algebraically closed constant extension is part of the proper-cover theory in SGA 1 and Stacks Project Section 58.9.

entries.title: Exactness of the Kummer sequence on the small étale site
entries.summary: When a positive integer is invertible on the scheme, taking its power on the multiplicative group is locally surjective in the étale topology.
statement:
Let $X$ be a scheme and $n>0$ an integer whose image in $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$ is a unit. The sheaves on the small étale site form an exact sequence
$$1\longrightarrow\mu_n\longrightarrow\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{(\cdot)^n}\mathbf G_m\longrightarrow1.$$
Here $\mu_n$ is the kernel of the $n$th-power map.

More concretely, every unit $a\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)^\times$ admits a root after a finite étale surjective morphism $f:Y\to X$: there is $b\in\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)^\times$ with $b^n=f^*a$. The cover can be chosen to have degree $n$ at every point.
discussion: An étale-local root need not descend to a global root. The long exact sequence relates this obstruction to roots-of-unity torsors and torsion in the Picard group, connecting equations for roots with line bundles. Classical Kummer theory studies field extensions obtained by extracting roots; the sheaf sequence carries that viewpoint to schemes, as developed in the Stacks Project.
history: Classical Kummer theory studies extensions obtained by extracting roots. The sheaf sequence extends that viewpoint from fields to schemes; Stacks Project Section 59.28 develops this formulation and its relation to Picard groups.

entries.title: Hilbert 90: vanishing of étale H¹ of Gₘ over characteristic-zero fields
entries.summary: The first étale cohomology of the multiplicative group vanishes over a characteristic-zero field.
statement:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero. For the multiplicative group sheaf on the small étale site of $\operatorname{Spec}K$, the theorem proves
$$H^1_{\mathrm{et}}(\operatorname{Spec}K,\mathbf G_m)=0.$$
Here $H^1$ denotes derived sheaf cohomology.
The current Lean theorem assumes characteristic zero; the classical vanishing statement holds over every field.
discussion: First cohomology of the multiplicative group classifies line bundles. Over a field, every one-dimensional vector space has a basis, so the corresponding line bundle is trivial. The étale formulation of Hilbert 90 places the classical field-theoretic vanishing within this Picard-group interpretation and connects multiplicative cocycles with descent. The classical theorem holds in every characteristic, beyond the characteristic-zero case stated here.
history: The étale formulation of Hilbert 90 places a field-theoretic vanishing result within the general identification of first multiplicative-group cohomology with the Picard group. Stacks Project Section 59.24 explains that identification.

entries.title: Finite étale schemes are equivalent to finite locally constant sheaves
entries.summary: The sheaf of sections identifies finite étale schemes with finite locally constant sheaves of sets on the small étale site.
statement:
For every scheme $X$, there is an equivalence
$$\operatorname{FinEt}(X)\simeq\mathbf{Sh}_{\mathrm{flc}}(X_{\mathrm{et}},\mathbf{Set}).$$
The right-hand category is the full subcategory of sheaves that are étale locally isomorphic to constant sheaves associated with finite sets.

The forward functor sends $Y\to X$ to its sheaf of sections, $U\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_X(U,Y)$. No connectedness, noetherianity, quasi-compactness, or assumption that $X$ lies over a field is included.
discussion: A finite cover can be viewed as a locally varying finite set whose gluing determines both the scheme and its morphisms. On a connected base with a geometric point, this also connects it to continuous finite fundamental-group actions. The correspondence is the algebraic analogue of the relation between covering spaces and locally constant sheaves in topology, expressed through étale representability.
history: This correspondence is the algebraic analogue of the relation between covering spaces and locally constant sheaves in topology. Stacks Project Lemma 59.64.4 gives the representability statement for the étale site.

entries.title: Proper henselian restriction is an isomorphism on H⁰ and injective on H¹
entries.summary: Restriction to the closed fiber is an isomorphism on H⁰ and injective on H¹ for any étale module sheaf on a proper scheme over a henselian local ring.
statement:
Let $R$ be a henselian local ring with residue field $\kappa$, let $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ be proper, and write $i:X_\kappa\to X$ for the closed-fiber inclusion. For any commutative coefficient ring $\Lambda$ and any étale sheaf $F$ of $\Lambda$-modules on $X$, restriction is bijective:
$$H^0(X_{\mathrm{et}},F)\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}H^0((X_\kappa)_{\mathrm{et}},i^*F).$$

For the same sheaf and coefficients, the actual restriction map in degree one is injective: $$H^1(X_{\mathrm{et}},F)\hookrightarrow H^1((X_\kappa)_{\mathrm{et}},i^*F).$$ No noetherianity or torsion condition is imposed. Surjectivity in degree one and the general higher-degree proper base change theorem are not asserted here.
discussion: Properness and the henselian base make the closed fiber sufficient for recovering global sections. In degree one, two classes that restrict to the same class were already equal on the original scheme. These conclusions hold with arbitrary module coefficients, without noetherianity or torsion assumptions.

The degree-one injectivity follows from the degree-zero comparison, an injective presentation, and exact direct image for the closed immersion. It is a step within proper base change theory; lifting every closed-fiber H¹ class remains a separate assertion.
history: Proper base change was developed in SGA 4 to control étale cohomology in families. Stacks Project Section 59.91 includes the degree-zero result for henselian pairs, with henselian local rings as a special case.

entries.title: Finite direct image is exact, commutes with base change, and preserves cohomology
entries.summary: A finite morphism has no positive higher direct images, commutes with arbitrary base change, and gives a coefficient-linear cohomology comparison in every degree.
statement: Let $f:X\to Y$ be finite, let $\Lambda$ be any commutative ring, and let $F$ be an étale sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules on $X$. Then
$$R^q f_*F=0\quad(q>0),\qquad H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,f_*F)\simeq_\Lambda H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,F)\quad(n\ge0).$$

For any $g:Y^{\prime}\to Y$, form the cartesian square with $X^{\prime}=X\times_Y Y^{\prime}$, projection $g^{\prime}:X^{\prime}\to X$, and $f^{\prime}:X^{\prime}\to Y^{\prime}$. The canonical base-change morphism is an isomorphism:
$$g^*f_*F\xrightarrow{\sim}f^{\prime}_*(g^{\prime})^*F.$$
No torsion condition on the coefficients, flatness, finite-presentation condition on f, or restriction on the base-change morphism is required. The cohomology comparison is natural in F.
discussion: Finite morphisms can be used to move an étale cohomology calculation to the base scheme without losing higher-degree information. Exactness of direct image removes the higher direct-image terms, and arbitrary base change makes this compatible with passing to fibers or changing the base.

The geometric stalk of finite direct image is a finite product of stalks over the fiber. This description underlies both exactness and the canonical base-change comparison; the Stacks Project presents these results in Proposition 59.55.2 and Lemma 59.55.3.
history: Finite direct images form a basic case of étale base change. Stacks Project Section 59.55 derives their higher vanishing and base-change behavior from the finite-fiber stalk description.
